The recently announced Section 301 investigations into 60+ countries suggest the administration’s goal is to fully replicate IEEPA tariffs with the more legally durable Section 301 authority. That said, we see two reasons why tariff rates could land lower than where they were before the IEEPA ruling: 1) Section 301 requires a public comment period, which typically leads to exclusions of key items, and 2) midterm elections could give the administration some pause in implementing the Section 301 tariffs quickly. The costs of war poses a bigger upside risk In addition to recent changes around tariffs, the war with Iran poses a meaningful and perhaps more durable upside risk to the deficit trajectory. The Department of Defense informed Congress that the actions taken over the first six days of the war cost $11.3bn, and Secretary Hegseth has asked for $200bn in supplemental funding. Importantly, Congress will need to approve any supplemental funding for defense. This helps explain why talks of a second reconciliation bill have picked up in recent days as Senate Democrats are unlikely to support more defense spending without some war limits being placed on the President. This has meant little demand for USD-higher option structures, reflecting a broad-based USD-bearish investor mindset. The sharp move higher in USD-call vol over the last three weeks (Figure 1) shows that heightened energy price risk has led investors to re- assess the value of these hedges. European epicentre: A sharp repricing in risk reversal skew is not limited to USD pairs, and Figure 2 shows the largest movers in the two weeks since the beginning of the Middle East conflict. European FX pairs as well as USDINR and USDKRW have been the biggest movers. In part, these moves reflect investor expectations that the EUR and other European currencies will be most affected by higher energy prices, but they also probably show the locations of positioning concentration, compelling a rapid repricing as hedges were added. records.text: EM FX | CORPORATE MARKETS MONTHLY The IDR appears less vulnerable within Asia to the oil shock, as Indonesia’s dependence on imported energy is relatively low. Moreover, the government is looking to make other spending cuts to maintain fuel-price controls, which could help retain fiscal credibility. Meanwhile, foreign ownership of local assets is historically low, which may reduce the potential impact of any slowdown in global portfolio flows caused by risk-off sentiment amid the Middle East conflict. The central bank may also intervene, given its explicit mandate to maintain financial stability. Overall, we expect any depreciation pressure in the IDR to be more modest than those faced by its peers. Macroeconomic fundamentals and monetary policy: Bank Indonesia kept its policy rate at 4.75% this month, citing the need to strengthen the persistently weak IDR. Meanwhile, domestic demand remained robust; in January, retail sales rose 5.7% y/y while loan growth continued to gain momentum, recording a 9.96% rise. Nevertheless, the Middle East tension and consequent oil shock could increase fragility in the economy. Headline inflation has been persistently rising, printing 4.76% in February, well above BI’s 2.5% target (±1%). Being a net- energy importer, albeit less-so than regional peers, would also risk further deteriorating Indonesia’s trade balance, which narrowed to a surplus of USD950mn in January from USD2.8bn in December. Prior to the conflict, we held a paid bias on THB and INR rates, due to favorable macroeconomic factors and our outlook for a bond demand–supply mismatch. Following the surge in oil prices and as rates moved higher quickly, we have taken profit on those positions and now running INR 1s5s steepener (see EM rates: Take profit on paid THOR 5y, dated 23 March, and EM rates: Take profit on INR 5y payer, enter 1s5s steepener, dated 11 March). If oil prices remain around current levels for an extended period of time, central banks may need to respond to keep inflation expectations anchored. As such, we may see further underperformance in the front end (e.g. 2y), as markets become increasingly convinced of a ‘proper’ hiking cycle over the next 24 months. This could lead to a divergence in curve dynamics, with the 1s2s segment steepening further. Furthermore, a prolonged elevation of oil prices would bring a risk of a negative growth shock to Asian economies, which would likely lead to a flattening of the rest of the curve the longer it persists. As markets price in a slowdown in economic growth and a potential reversal in monetary policies once inflation risks have been mitigated, the curve may continue to flatten, reflecting the expected slowdown over the medium term. Interestingly, the magnitude of UK inflation forecast revisions since the start of the war is comparable to that seen in the US following Liberation Day. It is worth highlighting that the upside inflation revisions in Europe have been particularly sharp and substantially larger than in the US. The US economy is less sensitive to moves in energy prices as it is a net energy exporter. Europe's heavy reliance on natural gas and electricity implies that the macro impact of the energy shock is amplified. While the pass- through of Brent oil prices to inflation is broadly similar for both Europe and the US, an increase in natural gas/energy prices has a materially larger effect on the Euro area and, even more so, on UK inflation. Larger inflation forecast revisions in Europe reflect not only higher oil prices but also the greater pass-through from elevated gas prices and, cru- cially, take into account that gas forward curves remain elevated over the coming months, whereas oil forwards decline much faster. L'utilisation d'options de change a considérablement augmenté, reflétant une demande accrue de solutions de couverture flexibles, bien que la hausse continue des prix de la volatilité ait encouragé certains à privilégier les structures de tunnel. L'affaiblissement inattendu du CHF et les commentaires de la BNS ont accru l'activité sur le CHF, certaines entreprises saisissant l'opportunité de prolonger leurs couvertures. Parallèlement, les niveaux d'activité ont augmenté dans les devises des marchés émergents, en particulier les paires à haut rendement et les pays fortement exposés aux prix de l'énergie (par exemple, HUF, BRL). Taux : La hausse des taux et l'aplatissement consécutif de la courbe ont d'abord surpris le marché et incité les entreprises à rester à l’écart. Cependant, au fur et à mesure que ce mouvement s’est développé, l'activité s'est intensifiée tant sur les ratios fixe/variable de dette que sur la pré-couverture des financements à venir. Comme lors des récentes périodes de volatilité des taux, les émetteurs s'aventurant sur les marchés de dette à leur réouverture ont opté pour des stratégies de pré- couverture à court terme – y compris intraday – pour protéger les coûts de financement contre des pics imprévus de hausse des taux de swaps. Morgan India Private Limited Global Markets Strategy U.S. Fixed Income Markets Weekly 27 March 2026 J P M O R G A N In terms of the K-shaped recovery, higher gas prices put a disproportionate burden on lower income. Additionally, lower income segments of the population generally have higher unemployment rates. Low-income borrowers may be more sensitive, with less savings/ cushion, against job loss. Broadly, we would still look for a roughly 1-for-1 relationship between unemployment versus defaults on prime and nonprime credit cards. With ABS structures, lower quality collateral pools should have more credit support (subordination and excess spread) against the higher expected losses. Where we would apply additional stress in running recession scenarios is with the seller/servicer risk. As we have seen in pre- vious economic cycles, a sponsor’s financial health and collateral performance goes hand- in-hand with ABS credit performance. Not only will charge-offs on ABS pools rise with unemployment, corporate (sponsor) default rates will rise in an economic recession 2. Issuer selection and sponsor spread tiering are essential in stress testing downside scenarios, along with labor market forecasts. Week in review There were only two new ABS pricings this week. records.text: Information Classification: General SPOTLIGHT FX VIEWS We are now nearly a month into the Middle East conflict. While EMFX sold off as investors aggressively reduced overweight positions ahead of the outbreak of war, the drawdowns have been modest relative to past geopolitical shocks such as the Russia–Ukraine war in 2022 or the COVID crisis in 2020. This resilience reflects limited downward global growth repricing, relatively contained USD strength, and improving EM fundamentals during the past decade . Local EM yield curves have generally bear-flattened, most notably at the front end, pointing to a repricing of central bank reaction functions rather than a deterioration in inflation expectations. Overall, markets are experiencing a risk -premium reset rather than a fundamental macro shock. Against this backdrop, we remain cautious near-term, staying selective and waiting for clearer re-entry points into pro-EM trades once sentiment improves. BRL remains our favourite pick in LatAm. Within LatAm, BRL remains our top pick, and the case extends beyond Brazil’s favourable oil exposure. Real rates remain highly attractive even after the recent rate cut and the rebound in 12 -month inflation expectations (Figure 2). COPOM delivered a unanimous 25bp cut last week, in line with market expectations. While the central bank left the door open to a faster pace of easing should external volatility decline meaningfully, its overall stance remains hawkish given Brazil’s macro backdrop of

As we argued in our Global Macro Year Ahead (see Global Macro Year Ahead: 2026: Attitude determines altitude), in the Euro area, the K-shape economy generated downside risks even before we consider the new shock. Wealth remains highly concentrated, but wealth effects have played a smaller role in K-shape recovery dynamics since 2020. Excess savings accrued during pandemic years were largely confined to the wealthiest quintile while the 2022 inflation surge disproportionately affected lower-income households, eroding real incomes. records.text: inflation forwards, the inflation accrual of TIPS during an energy-driven inflation surge can still be beneficial. We use our backcasted TIPS series and actual data to estimate and analyze how TIPS have fared during past supply-driven oil shocks of similar magnitude. Intuitively, our estimates suggest that breakevens tend to widen while oil is rising and subsequently moderate when oil is past the peak (Exhibit 3). The sharper and more durable instances of breakeven widening in our estimates took place during the 1970s episodes alongside a more persistent rise in underlying inflation and longer-term inflation expectations, whereas the two more recent experiences of 1990 and 2022 saw breakevens (estimated in 1990 and realized in 2022) settle at lower levels six-to-twelve months after the shock compared to where they went in. This paper provides a framework for detecting bubbles in assets based on their price action. The model works by drawing on the tendency for asset prices in a bubble regime to repeat certain behaviours: ▪ Building momentum: A bubble is most clearly defined as an upward move in price as momentum builds. The rise of the asset price attracts further asset flows, which pushes the asset price up further. A positive feedback loop is created. ▪ Periodic oscillation: Another defining feature of bubbles can be found in short periods of price drawdown, creating mini boom-bust cycles. Typical price behaviour in bubbles is that the peaks and troughs of these cycles become more pronounced, and the frequency of the cycles increases, until a ‘critical time’ at which the bubble can no longer be sustained. Mathematically this process is described in the equation in Figure 1. An illustrative example is shown in Figure 2. The LPPLS approach fits this equation many times, over different time horizons. This appears to be a response to skepticism about whether a rate hike is really necessary with energy subsidies and other measures under the Takaichi administration recently pushing core inflation well below 2%. records.text: Ning Sun 26 March 2026 1 Insights Information Classification: General Familiar shock, unusual starting point for EMFX Since the outbreak of the Iran conflict, EMFX have come under sustained pressure. Nearly a month into the escalation in the Middle East, EMFX has been sold off quite aggressively as energy prices jumped and uncertainty around the duration and scope of the conflict remains high. Figure 1 compares EMFX performance during four major shocks: the 2013 Taper Tantrum, the 2014 OPEC oil shock, COVID-19 in 2020, and the 2022 Russia–Ukraine war. It shows cumulative changes in the MSCI EMFX Index over approximately 85 trading days from each event's start. The current EMFX selloff following the Iran war is notable but consistent with these past events, generally tracking the lower end of historical outcomes at this stage. Of course, each shock has had its own unique transmission channels into EMFX. For example, the Taper Tantrum was primarily a U.S. policy-driven interest rate shock, while COVID-19 represented an abrupt global risk-off and growth collapse. But what makes this episode fundamentally different, however, is the starting point from a positioning perspective. Our historical positioning data suggest that EMFX entered the current shock with positioning around the 85th percentile , meaning investors were heavily overweight EM relative to the past 5 years. Sentiment is starting to show its effects already Our concerns about the “fresh memory” of confidence were fuelled by consumer confidence data this week. The European Commission’s “flash” consumer confidence index deteriorated by 4 points in March. The shallow recovery of last year has once again reversed. Business sentiment held up a little better – as seen in Ifo, INSEE and Istat surveys. And so did manufacturing PMIs, although caution is warranted. Supply delivery times have increased sharply and, by construction, that’s a positive for manufacturing PMIs. Excluding those, PMIs would have declined (Exhibit 1). Fiscal policy: shock absorber or shock amplifier A common feature in recent discussions has been the fiscal response. Spain has started with a c EUR5bn package, and its effect on energy prices could be relatively sizeable, at least in the short term. By comparison, Italy’s 20-day pump price subsidy may get washed out. France has implemented targeted support for agriculture, fishing and transport services (although more liquidity support than proper cash). More may be in the making, but we doubt we will see big changes. Germany is, as so often, an outlier. The government has enacted legislation that restricts the number of price rises at pump stations. When it comes to future monetary policy, rate hikes would be straightforward to envision if the unemployment rate were steadily declining. In contrast, the Fed last tightened monetary policy on a sustained basis into clearly rising unemployment during the early 1980s, under then-Chair Volcker, to regain inflation-fighting credibility. We believe the Fed would only raise rates into a growth-negative shock like the Middle East conflict if this were perceived as necessary to mount a similar credibility defense. While this is not our base case, we feel it cannot be ruled out given the context of a stimulative monetary policy stance, the prolonged US inflation overshoot and the unknown nature of the energy price shock.

By combining core inflation that, excluding special factors, still exceeds 2% with an output gap that remains positive, the BoJ can argue to some extent that current inflation has not only cost-push but also has demand-pull elements. One provision in the 21st Century ROAD to Housing Act, which the Senate passed earlier this month and now awaits a House vote, would strike five words—“built on a permanent chassis”—from the federal definition of a manufactured home. Manufactured homes have been required to be built on a steel chassis—a trailer frame that remains attached even after it is installed on a site—since Congress passed the Man- ufactured Home Construction and Safety Standards Act of 1974 (hereafter, the HUD Code). Critics say this requirement adds cost and enables localities to exclude these homes from residential areas by classifying them as mobile structures. The chassis requirement has been cited as a key reason the market share of manufactured homes fell from over 25% of production in the early 1970s to 6% today (Figure 1). Howev- er, mobile home shipments as a share of housing starts had already declined 13%-pt in the previous half-decade before the HUD Code took effect in 1976. Recessions in the 1970s hit the industry harder than conventional construction. The market share of manufactured homes fell a further 14%-pt in the late-1990s following a wave of loan defaults that prompt- ed many specialty lenders to exit the business entirely. 0 5 10 15 20 25 30 60 65 70 75 80 85 90 95 00 05 10 15 20 25 % Figure 1: Shipments of mobile homes as a share of housing starts Source: Census Manufactured Housing Survey, J.P. records.text: Japan Outlook BoJ justifies normalization path with new CPI and output gap indicators BoJ’s new core CPI ex-special factors remains above 2% and its revised output gap shows positive for 15 consecutive quarters, drastically changing recent assessments. These justify its normalization path and imply an almost preset course toward an April hike absent Middle East conflict. BoJ releases new indicators for CPI inflation and output gap On 26 March, the BoJ released indicators of CPI inflation excluding special factors and a new output gap estimate. At the 19 March monetary policy meeting, Governor Ueda had said that the BoJ would like to publish these, as well as re-estimation results for the natural rate of interest, as soon as they are ready. With the next Outlook Report due for release at the coming April meeting, the BoJ appears to have prioritized communications on the CPI and output gap. Setting aside the impact of the Middle East conflict, these releases work in the direction of justifying the BoJ’s normalization path. Excluding special factors, core inflation remains above 2% In the new CPI inflation indicators, special factors stemming from institutional changes are excluded. Specifically, at this stage, the excluded items are the consumption tax, free education policies, the mobile phone fee cuts (2021), travel support programs and energy subsidies. records.text: CORPORATE MARKETS MONTHLY 426/03/2026 G10 FX USD: The energy shock is bullish for the USD, contrary to our previous base case in which we expected the USD to lose ground against the EUR and EM high-yielders. EUR: As the eurozone is a net energy importer, the shock is bearish for the EUR, weighing on the trade balance and growth. The European Central Bank could hike rates if elevated energy prices persist. However, we do not expect the hikes to be beneficial for the currency, as they would be associated with weaker growth. JPY: The JPY is also vulnerable to higher energy prices, as Japan is an energy importer. Renewed inflation pressure in Japan could reinforce the perception that the Bank of Japan is lagging behind the curve, a factor we see as a continued source of yen weakness. GBP: In the UK, the shock adds to the bearish impact on the GBP of political uncertainty ahead of the May local elections. The spike in energy prices creates significant doubt about the scope for further Bank of England rate cuts, and the associated growth downside further bolsters GBP weakness, in our view. While these are still early days, we see limited evidence that the global oil shock will broaden into a material hit to domestic activity, however. Of course, as we wrote last week, this view hinges on the assumption that consumers remain shielded from higher ener- gy prices through subsidies. And, crucially, that manufactur- ers do not face volume constraints on the supply of energy or other key inputs that could materially affect factory output. Against this backdrop, the March flash PMI survey pointed to some slowing ahead, with relatively large drops in new orders and future output indicators, consistent with our forecast for a pullback in 2Q growth. On the flip side, domestic indicators continue to hint at robust momentum. The agreed hike in base pay in the initial rounds of Shunto negotiations was strong this week, averaging just over 3.8%, almost unchanged from last year’s already-elevated rate. With corporate profit growth remaining solid, supported in part by sustained yen weakness, we continue to think Japan’s private sector has space for fur- ther wage hikes. Rising wages, solid demand, and a second- round impact from higher global energy prices suggest under- lying inflation will remain firm, even as subsidies suppress some core inflation measures through mid year. Par-weighted spreads for indexed Software names have widened ~13bps since YE compared to ~2bps for Semiconductors, a divergence that reflects fundamentally different AI cycle exposure. Semis are direct beneficiaries as infrastructure buildouts drive sustained demand for advanced compute, high-bandwidth memory, and the broader silicon stack, showing up in credit as spread stability and in some cases outright tightening. records.text: gy Gold Revisiting the other drivers Gold trade represents a distinctive aspect of Türkiye’s exter- nal balance dynamics. Turkish households have historically regarded gold as an inflation hedge, resulting in net gold imports being a significant and volatile component of the cur- rent account. As real returns on lira deposits decline, there is a corresponding shift in demand toward gold, which in turn increases gold imports. Our modeling approach specifies net gold imports as a function of real interest rates, while control- ling for global gold prices. The analysis finds that a 10%-pt decline in real rates widens the current account balance by $5.2 billion, or 0.3% of GDP. The gold balance is estimated to exert additional, albeit moderate, pressure on the current account. Beyond energy and gold, the current account is expected to come under additional pressure from real lira appreciation, though this will be partially offset by slower credit growth in 2026 (Table 1 and 2).The CBRT’s ongoing strategy of utiliz- ing real lira appreciation as a disinflation anchor is anticipat- ed to stimulate import demand, thereby widening the core current account deficit. Morgan Securities plc Nicolaie Alexandru-Chidesciuc(44 20) 7742-2466 nicolaie.alexandru@jpmorgan.com Global Economic Research 27 March 2026 J P M O R G A N geopolitical risk, the rise in energy prices and potential risks to financial market stability all justify keeping rates unchanged at 6.25%, the central bank argued. The NBH lifted its inflation projection to 3.8% in 2026 (from 3.2%) and 3.7% in 2027 (from 3.3%), still counting on a return to the 3%oya target mid-point in 2028. Like the CNB’s communication last week, the NBH signaled caution more than hawkishness. The statement says a “careful and patient” approach is necessary, and that maintaining tight monetary conditions is warranted. It argues further that in this environment, it is crucial to stabilize domestic financial mar- kets, especially currency markets. In the press conference, Governor Varga said FX stability is indispensable and that the NBH reserves the right to intervene in the FX market, a state- ment which is not so typical of the NBH. What about the fiscal response? We don’t expect the fiscal response to be as forceful as in 2022, given the limited fiscal space. The move higher in yields along with potential weaker growth is likely to have already hurt the headroom. 10-year gilt yields are ~40bps higher than the OBR’s March forecast, which would likely reduce the headroom by ~£5bn from current £23.6bn. We don’t expect the Chancellor to break or suspend the fiscal rules. Moreover, the bar for universal support such as an energy price guarantee is high. Targeted temporary support costing low single-digit billions looks more likely. This could be done by delaying the September fuel duty rise (costing £600mn) or targeted support to low-income households (via an expanded Warm Homes Discount, which is a £150 discount currently on electricity bills for people on Pension Credit and certain benefits or welfare-based payments). It is also possible that the Chancellor takes more policy costs off bills to lower the rise in the July cap. The bar for an energy price guarantee is high – we think it is only possible in more adverse scenarios of much higher energy bills especially in the winter. The court is allowing the administration time to set up the refund program and process, but the quick ruling suggests that these refunds could hit the deficit towards the end of this fiscal year (Sep 2026) and throughout FY27. We hope to learn more on the timing and process when Customs and Border Protection reports its progress to the courts on March 31. Given the relatively quick action by the court and the cooperation by the administration, we expect that the bulk of the refunds will likely go out in FY 2027. records.text: ations, and sovereignty over the Strait of Hormuz. 3 Meanwhile, signals from Trump have been mixed, praising negotiations but also doubting if a deal can be achieved 4 . The US administration is also preparing military escalation options, including the use of ground forces, as expeditionary and airborne forces are being moved to the region. 5 The communication around the war remains challenging for markets to interpret. Markets price inflationary and fiscal consequences... With Gulf energy infrastructure damaged, oil and other commodity shipments through the Strait reduced to a trickle, and no clear signs of an imminent deescalation, oil and gas prices have remained volatile and elevated. Brent traded around $110 per barrel at the time of writing. In parallel, developed market yields, particularly in the front end, sold off a little further this week, leaving core 2y rates 60-100bp higher than before the war. Markets are thus pricing immediate inflationary consequences, to which they expect central banks to react with hikes. Medium- and long-term yields are also significantly higher, as markets demand additional term premium against longer-term risks to fiscal dynamics and more inflation uncertainty. The pressure on longer yields was especially felt in the UK but also elsewhere. Unlike markets, economic data typically react with a lag, and it will take some time to see the full effects of the war. However, incoming releases offer the first glimpses into the economic imprints

records.text: rgence between input and output prices - an early indication of margin compression This week, we began to see the Middle East conflict feeding through to key macro variables. The Government responded by cutting oil excise duties sharply to keep pump prices unchanged, which increases the risks to fiscal deficit fore- casts. Recall that pump prices in India have remained flat despite the sharp rise in crude prices. The Minister indicated that full pass-through has not occurred, implying that if oil prices remain elevated—or rise further—the Government will likely need to either cut excise duties further or allow pump price hikes. Meanwhile, incoming activity indicators are showing early signs of strain. The manufacturing flash PMI fell to a 4.5-year low in March with both the output index and forward-looking new orders witnessing large falls. The PMI details also point to rising input costs alongside softer output prices, suggesting margin compression for manufacturers. Government cuts oil excise duty The Government has announced a Rs10 per liter cut in central excise duty on petrol and diesel (Figure 1). Pump prices will remain unchanged, with the measure aimed at supporting Government-owned Oil Marketing Companies (OMCs) that are currently absorbing losses as retail prices have not kept pace with higher crude prices. Western Europe CBs all rise The energy shock began to show up in Western European economic releases this week. Output and future output indices fell in the March PMI, while the output price index rose. Spanish inflation accelerated 1%-pt 0.8%-pt on a HICP basis. For the ECB lower output expectations are a concern, but the ECB views downside risks as limited with German fiscal pol- icy support gearing up. For the BoE the sharp increase in household longer-term inflation expectations to 4.6% for March is a material worry, particularly with wage and core CPI inflation running above BoE expectations. Commentary from both central banks is mixed on the prospects for early rate hikes, but we judge the case will build if there is no de- escalation in the Middle East conflict. Modest reflation in China China’s economy remains relatively resilient to the current energy shock, supported by high inventory levels, a diversi- fied energy mix, and multiple sourcing channels. The main near-term impact of the energy shock is likely to be on infla- tion. EM BOND WATCH 2yr Mbono spread widening driven mainly by real Figure 6 Mbono vs UST 2yr differential breakdown The two-year segment of the yield curve is closely tied to the monetary policy cycle. During this month’s selloff, the 2y Mbono/UST yield differential widened by about 40bps, driven primarily by a sharp move in real yield differentials, while breakeven differentials remained relatively stable. Liquidity effects explain part of the jump —Mexican Udibonos are less liquid than US TIPS—but the divergence between volatile real rates and stable breakevens suggests markets are not meaningfully repricing Mexico–US inflation differentials. Instead, the move reflects a repricing of central bank reaction functions, with markets expecting a more hawkish Banxico relative to the Fed. This is consistent with interest rate swap pricing, where rate cuts for Mexico have now been fully priced out. Given Mexico’s still -high real rates and weakening growth momentum, the front end looks attractive, providing there is a reasonable headline risk de-escalation. Morgan Securities LLC Global Markets Strategy U.S. Fixed Income Markets Weekly 27 March 2026 J P M O R G A N Primary rate surveys may be masking a bigger backup in refi rates The backup in rates, higher implied vol, and the current coupon drifting from a 4.5/5 mix to the wider OAS 5/5.5 blend have all pushed mortgage rates higher. At first glance, howev- er, the primary/secondary spread (P/SS) appears to have compressed and acted as a dampen- er on this move. That’s not unusual, historically—the P/SS typically widens into rallies as volumes surge and margins expand, and shrinks into selloffs as originators fight for busi- ness. That being said, we were surprised that there was room for 10bp of compression when origination gain-on-sale margins (per Q4 data) weren’t particularly lofty. The 2022 Party Congress then formalized the shift by enshrining these practices and policies in Party doctrine, com- pleting the break from the previous decades (China 3.0). Best laid plans of mice and men But things didn't quite unfold as Beijing had hoped. China has indeed tightened its regulatory framework, from environmen- tal rules to financial oversight, and both economic growth and leverage have slowed (Figure 1). But the economic challeng- es have intensified. The much-anticipated shift from a hous- ing-driven economy to one powered by high-end manufactur- ing remains incomplete. The property market’s downturn has now stretched into its fifth year. Although advanced manufac- turing has posted impressive gains, it hasn’t been enough to offset the drag from real estate, hampered by obstacles on both the supply and demand sides. We think the economy is still in this latter phase. Decompositions from the San Francisco Fed show that rising utilization has accounted for much of the productivity pickup over the past year ( Figure 3)—a source of growth that is unlikely to be durable. Adjusting for this, productivity growth in 2025 appears closer to 1.6–2.0%, depending on the output measure used. That is modestly above our late‑2024 estimate of structural productivity growth (1.7%), but well short of a regime shift. Capital deepening, meanwhile, has contributed little to recent gains. Despite prominent headlines about AI hyperscaler capex, aggregate capital accumulation remains slow by historical standards ( Figure 4), reflecting weak investment across the rest of the economy. Business fixed investment rose a pedestrian 5.5% Q4/Q4 in 2025, while non‑AI‑sensitive components fell 3.6%. We doubt this reflects understatement of AI capex; if anything, hyperscaler tallies are more likely to double‑count spending or include items that do not qualify as NIPA investment. For what its worth, the flash PMI for March this week showed a large rise in input pricing components but also a four point drop in output expectations. The biggest surprise was a sharp move higher in the Citi/You Gov longer term measure of household inflation expectations from 3.6% to 4.5% (versus a 4.8%) peak in 2022. The real information ahead of April will come from whether energy prices stay at current levels or not. This week’s narrowing is more than would be implied by fundamentals, as 5- and 10- year breakevens now appear 16bp and 17bp, respectively, too narrow after adjusting for broad commodity prices, the forward OIS curve as a proxy for macro sentiment, and the VIX Index as a measure of risk appetite (Figure 3B r e a k e v e n s o n c e m o r e a p p e a r m o r e t h a n a s t a n d a r d d e v i a t i o n c h e a p t o f u n d a m e n t a l s ). This is more than a standard deviation cheap in our framework. Second, inflation markets are pricing in a quick resolution to the conflict with limited impact from from the oil price shock beyond the next few months, as headline m/m CPI is projected to converge with the pre-conflict forecast path by May (see Monthly Inflation Outlook, Francis Diamond, 3/25/26). records.text: le together support for a party-line reconciliation bill that includes more defense spending, it would not surprise us to see other provisions included that would drive up the cost. For example, Congress could suspend the gas tax, an idea the President has supported, to provide some relief to households. This could add around $40bn/year to the deficit. Republicans in competitive midterm races would presumably push for more significant consumer relief. In thinking about the deficit impact of a potential reconciliation bill, any consumer relief is likely to be immediate due to the midterms. Based on prior supplemental bills for Ukraine and Israel, we think allocated increases in the defense budget would take time to fully be spent (Exhibit 3). That said, the costs of war could change significantly if the war continues for longer than expected and if it involves actual troops on the ground. For example, the costs of the Afghanistan, Iraq & Syria wars averaged more than $100bn/year in 2025$ (Exhibit 4). That would likely shift the narrative in markets back to concerns over debt levels in the US and could pressure the long end of the curve higher, given limited demand and the need to grow coupon issuance earlier than currently expected.

records.text: China: March PMIs next week could confirm the economy's resilience In contrast, we may get a little more direction from next week's data in Asia. After a solid start to the year judging by January-February activity data, we will get China's March PMIs, which we expect to reaffirm the country's relative resilience to the global energy shock as both manufacturing and non-manufacturing gauges improve, with the latter returning to expansionary territory. Unlike in many other regions, China's government price controls imply a limited pass-through to domestic fuel prices. So far, we estimate that only about 20% of the global crude price increase has been reflected in China's domestic gasoline prices. Moreover, China ordered an immediate ban on refined fuel exports on 12 March to preempt any potential domestic fuel shortage. At the same time, China may even benefit from its exports of green technology if the war prompts other countries to invest more in alternative energy sources to address vulnerabilities. ... and central banks focus on communication ECB further explains its strategy At this week's ECB Watchers Conference, President Lagarde reiterated the bank's agility to respond but again stopped short of pre-committing to an April hike. All three stressed the value of acting when more information about the nature of the inflationary shock was available, with Deputy Governor Breeden highlighting that there are two-sided risks to inflation. As we discussed last week, since the start of the Iran conflict, market expecta- tions for the Fed have shifted hawkishly, and policy uncertainty has increased (Interest Rate Derivatives, U.S. Fixed Income Markets Weekly, 3/20/2026). Figure 1 shows the market- implied probabilities of various Fed policy scenarios through year end, as inferred from options on Dec'26 3M SOFR futures. On the day before the start of the conflict, markets considered it very unlikely that the Fed would hike this year, assigning a probability of less than 10%. The market-implied probability that the Fed would cut at least twice this year was ~50%. Since then, the implied distribution has changed drastically: the left (low-rate) tail has weakened, and a significant right tail has developed. At present, the market-implied probability of 1 or more cuts by year end is only 30%, and markets now assign high probabilities to hike scenarios, ~15% for 1 hike and ~35% for 2+ hikes. If energy prices are high enough for long enough to justify the BoE no longer cutting rates but moving instead to a hike to curb inflation, we think it would be associated with a significant hit to UK growth. We therefore do not consider rate differentials a supportive factor for the GBP. Our analysis suggests that until now, GBPUSD has outperformed past sensitivities to oil shocks significantly (Figure 2). Following the methodology used in FX and energy Q&A: Strait answers, dated 12 March, we find that past betas of GBPUSD to oil shocks would imply a move of -4.5% (with oil going from USD70/bbl to USD115/bbl). However, since 27 February, GBPUSD has fallen by 1.5% (as of 19 March), implying more room for GBPUSD downside, were energy prices to stay high for longer. In addition to the energy shock, UK political uncertainty remains. A change of Labour Party leadership remains a source of uncertainty ahead of local elections in May. The main risk for the market is that a change in leadership could lead to a government less committed to fiscal prudence than previously (see UK politics: Succession scenarios, dated 13 February). Macroeconomic fundamentals and monetary policy: The BoE remained on hold at the March meeting, as it chose to err on the side of caution amid rising energy prices and geopolitical uncertainty. records.text: G10 FX | CORPORATE MARKETS MONTHLY 1226/03/2026 NOK VIEW SEK VIEW NOK and SEK: Oil driving divergence We have placed our NOK and SEK forecasts under review, given geopolitical developments. We see the rise in oil prices as likely to cause divergence between the NOK and SEK due to differences in energy trade balances and inflation starting points. Norway is a net energy exporter with a net energy trade balance worth 21% of GDP in 2024, the highest in the G10. Norway’s inflation is running above target, and the country has recently seen upside surprises in its inflation prints (Figure 1). Additional inflationary pressure therefore creates a risk of further tightening. Sweden, in contrast, is a net energy importer, with an energy trade deficit worth 1.2% of GDP in 2024. A rise in oil prices should worsen its current account and weaken the SEK. Prior to the oil price shock, Sweden was in a position of below-target inflation with concerns about undershooting projections. While higher oil prices are likely to add inflationary pressure, with inflation currently weak, we think the market may instead focus on the negative growth impact. Macroeconomic fundamentals and monetary policy: Previously, the tone around Norges Bank meetings implied caution towards further easing, as inflation is sticky and above target. This development raises concerns regarding a deterioration in the current account, which could threaten FX stability and under- mine Türkiye's disinflation efforts in 2026. Our assessment anticipates a widening of the current account deficit, primarily driven by higher oil prices and real lira appreciation; however, we expect the CA deficit to remain manageable. records.text: G10 RATES | CORPORATE MARKETS MONTHLY 3026/03/2026 USD rates: Geopolitics poses upside risks to yields Fed on hold through to year end: We still expect the US Federal Reserve to remain on hold this year, owing to US economic resilience and high, sticky inflation. February nonfarm payrolls fell by 92k, but this largely reflected severe weather that hurt certain sectors and a widespread strike by nurses in California. The uptick in the unemployment rate likely leaves the Fed retaining an easing bias for now, but hawkish officials will probably still emphasize that this indicator was lower at the start of 2026 than in Q4 2025. Meanwhile, the Middle East conflict has created a negative supply shock as the Strait of Hormuz remains constrained. The large and ongoing rise in energy prices, and lack of clarity on its likely duration, means US inflation could run hot and for a prolonged period. This leaves an underappreciated tail risk that the Fed moves toward a "symmetric policy bias", i.e. either a rate hike or a cut is roughly equally likely to follow. Since the conflict started, markets have removed more than one cut from 2026 Fed pricing, while other global central banks have seen hikes priced in. Overall, a stable labor market, sticky price growth, and no imminent signs of either de-escalation in the conflict or effective circuit breakers for energy prices should see cuts get priced out, dragging front-end yields higher. The Fed backdrop likely limits the pressure on EM central bankers who are often forced to hike due to pressures from currencies or rising global interest rates. In most cases, poli- cymakers have time to assess the nature of the shock. Absent market pressures, they will hike only after they see evidence of a firming in underlying inflation or a dislodging of CPI/ wage expectations. The main outlier to this cautious hawkish tilt is in Europe where we expect hikes next quarter from the ECB, BoE, Riksbank and NorgesBank. There are different motivations for hikes, with the BoE more sensitive to inflation expecta- tions while the ECB is sensitive to its projections that energy shocks will have a persistent core inflation pass-through. But the common factor is a downplaying of concerns that they might magnify a regional growth drag, even as they recognize the potential for a large negative shock. Tail risks and vulnerabilities The immediate concerns regarding energy supply constraints are concentrated in Asia where dependence on Middle East imports is greatest. India has begun energy rationing for com- mercial establishments, while the Philippines and Vietnam have declared national emergencies. Shortages remain con- fined to the petrochemical industry, but broader shutdowns will accompany a prolonged period of reduced imports. From a performance perspective, 1s5s Latam curve steepeners have produced positive Sharpe ratios during past oil-price shocks, but they still rank among the lowest in the broader EM universe. For outright positions, the rally in Latam rates after oil-price peaks tends to cause outright payers to underperform during the two-month window following the oil-price peak. Although steepeners in Latam are generally less appealing on a risk-return basis than those in other EM markets, Brazil’s domestic story could support a steepener position, we think. records.text: E M – L O C A L E YE S FO R A G L O B A L V IE W 626/03/2026 Curve steepening amid oil shocks: For Latam, the local curve behavior during oil-shock episodes largely mirrors that of its EM counterparts – the curve bear steepens and the asset swap spreads tighten. In particular, 1s5s steepeners in Mexico, Chile and Colombia consistently outperformed, delivering positive returns during the shock, albeit followed by a less clear trend post the peak oil price (Latam: How to trade oil shocks?). What stands out the most for Latam versus the rest of EM is that when shocks are extreme, the reversal of the sell-off in rates is the sharpest as well. Hence, the growth trade-off is most obvious for Latam rates, with 1s2s being the main part of the curve that flattens in extreme shocks (Figure 21). Fiscal vulnerability prevents flattening beyond the 2y point: We view high fiscal vulnerability as the main factor causing the curves to fail to flatten initially and to experience a pronounced steepening unless there’s a risk of severe demand destruction. Most Latam economies are net oil exporters with little fiscal slack. During oil-price spikes, markets are reassured by rising revenues and limited growth fallout. Once prices retreat, fiscal pressure from government subsidies or stimulus keeps the curve steep, especially in 2s5s, highlighting the Latam curve’s strong sensitivity to fiscal risk and its slow unwind. Fading prospects for an imminent reopening of the Strait of Hormuz reinforce our loosely articulated baseline scenario but also raise tail risk concerns. The baseline envisions an extended disruption that sustains Brent crude through midyear. If followed by a receding of tensions that push oil to $80bbl, we estimate 2026 global growth will be lowered by 0.6% and CPI inflation raised by 1%. But the longer the Strait remains closed, the sharper the draw-down in buffer supplies that could spark dramatic increases in the price of crude oil, natural gas and other commodities. A scenario in which the Strait remains closed for an additional month would be consistent with crude oil prices rising towards $150bbl and constraints on industrial consumers of energy supply. The threat of a stagflationary tilt is being reflected in financial markets, where bond yields have moved higher this month, at the same time that equities have incorporated greater growth concerns. Tightening monetary policy and rising inflation risk premia are a hallmark of earlier energy supply shocks, and significant pressure on yields would magnify the modest growth drag in our baseline scenario. records.text: ECB well positioned to act At The ECB and Its Watchers conference, ECB President Christine Lagarde discussed the similarities and differences of the current energy shock from the one generated by the Russian invasion of Ukraine, the ECB's scenarios and the strategy to cope with the new shock. She concluded: "We will not act before we have sufficient information on the size and persistence of the shock and its propagation. But we will not be paralysed by hesitation: our commitment to delivering 2% inflation over the medium term is unconditional" . In our view, the outlook for the energy shock is unlikely to be consistent with the ECB's baseline forecast. Whether the euro area macroeconomic landscape ultimately aligns more closely with the adverse or the severe scenario will depend on both the magnitude and the persistence of the shock. As such, we continue to think that the Governing Council will act sooner rather than later to recalibrate the monetary policy stance and increase policy rates by 25bp at the April and June meetings. records.text: Euro Area Outlook First imprints The war in the Middle East is leaving its first imprints on activity and price developments. We interpret latest ECB communication as supporting a first rate hike in April if the energy shock persists. We continue to expect a second 25bp hike at the June meeting. • March PMIs point to 1) a weakening of demand across countries and in the services sector in• particular; 2) a sizeable increase in input prices, partly passed through to output prices; and 3) signs of supply bottlenecks. Consumer confidence also dropped considerably in March. • Inflation accelerated in Spain in March, but less than expected (HICP at 3.3% y/y; Barclays• forecast: 3.9%; Bloomberg consensus: 3.8% y/y; February: 2.5% y/y). We expect higher energy prices to lift headline inflation in the euro area in March (to be released on 31 March) by around 0.7pp to 2.6% y/y. We project a deceleration in core inflation of 0.1pp to 2.3% y/y. • If spot and forward energy prices remain as elevated as currently, we would expect the ECB to• increase policy rates by 25bp at the 30 April meeting. In contrast, we were bullish on other pairs such as USDJPY, where Japan’s fiscal picture looks worrisome. However, this base case excluded geopolitical escalations. We will review our FX forecasts once a new base case feels sufficiently comfortable, but for now, we acknowledge the path to realize our prior outlook seems much narrower. We see room for USD upside to persist as time passes as the longer that energy prices stay at current elevated levels the positive effects on the USD can accumulate. The US is an energy exporter, so higher prices are USD- bullish through the terms of trade channel, especially against the eurozone and Asia, which are importers. In addition, we estimate that the hit to growth from sustained higher energy prices is less to the US than to those importers, in turn implying that front-end rate differentials should widen in favor of the USD as well. records.text: ab 29 March 2026 Global Research Global Strategy Our 2026 Private Credit Outlook: Key Client Questions Executive Summary: Responding to Key Client Debates We provide an update on our 2026 private credit outlook, including answers to key client questions in our recent conversations. On the Middle East, we believe that private credit is unlikely to be fundamentally derailed unless we face an extended disruption scenario severe enough to trigger a sharp oil-driven recession. We expect private credit valuation marks to move closer to broadly syndicated loan comparables as liquidity pressures rise via higher redemptions. Recovery rates across leveraged loans and private credit have already fallen meaningfully, and our baseline outlook assumes the potential for higher defaults and structurally lower recoveries at 35% in leveraged loans and 30% in private credit. These dynamics could spill over into structured credit through reduced loan and CLO issuance, the possibility of higher downgrade pressure, and greater ratings sensitivity for mezzanine CLO tranches. Finally, we show that private credit has played an increasingly central role in US non-financial credit creation, implying that private credit weakness could have an adverse effect on broad credit growth How does Middle East escalation affect our Private Credit outlook? Morgan Securities LLC Global Markets Strategy Global Fixed Income Markets Weekly 27 March 2026 J P M O R G A N At the risk of repeating ourselves, the increase in implieds over the past month has been driven by risk-off sentiment due to the current geopolitical backdrop. Indeed, our UST strat- egists have written about the impact of the decline in liquidity on risk sentiment and market depth, noting that persistent delivered volatility has led to a deterioration in market depth (see US Treasury Market Daily, 3/25/2026). Looking ahead, we remain cautious on volatility. Implieds have increased to sufficiently high levels that our empirical model for long gamma returns (which accounts for the recent relationship with equity returns) points to statistically significant negative returns. Howev- er, we are hesitant to fade the move as the uncertain macro backdrop remains, and next week also brings more event risk associated with the payrolls print. As we noted last week, when there is more clarity on the geopolitical backdrop, we'll look to position for normalization of the vol surface, as the 6M-expiry 2s/30s vol curve still appears to be elevated (Figure 9). records.text: ment • The labor market has been buffeted by shocks to supply (immigration restrictions) and demand (tariff uncertainty, AI, DOGE). In our view, the supply shock is likely to be the bigger driver of soft job growth this year, especially as labor demand starts to recover on the back of fading tariff uncertainty, a positive fiscal policy impulse and consumer resilience. Hence, we have payrolls averaging 50k in 2026. Immigration tightening likely lowers breakeven job growth to about 20k, keeping payrolls close to full employment. Hence, we see the u-rate at 4.5% in 2Q26 and then dropping to 4.3% by 4Q26. Fed: two cuts in 2026 but on hold under Powell • The Fed held rates steady at 3.5-3.75% at its Mar meeting, as expected. In the characterization of current conditions, the Fed emphasized that the economic implications of the Iran war are uncertain. Powell’s comments discussed at length the ongoing inflation overshoot and upside risks to inflation, but barely discussed downside risks to the labor market. We remain comfortable with our view that the Fed won’t cut again under Powell. We have penciled in two 25bp cuts under the next Chair (Kevin Warsh), with low conviction, in June and July for a terminal rate of 3.0- 3.25%. Policy under the next Chair will depend a lot on the FOMC composition.

But if growth remains strong (with tech continuing to surge) and inflation pressures progressively build, the CBC could turn its gaze more decisively towards inflation as 2026 progresses. There is, however, a second set of economies that have rela- tively fewer energy buffers and are less insulated from shut- downs. This group includes the Philippines, India, Thailand and Indonesia. These central banks will be much more con- cerned about an immediate hit to growth and, therefore, are more likely to adopt a 2020 COVID playbook: prioritize growth over inflation in the near term and pursue sector-spe- cific regulatory and liquidity support. Coming into this shock, inflation has been very benign in the region – indicative of slack in several of Asia’s economies – reinforcing the instinct to be patient. The tension for some central banks in being dovish is that, unlike COVID, external imbalances have wors- ened because of higher energy prices and, combined with capital outflows, currencies have been under pressure. • In India, we expect the RBI to be patient, and growth supportive, among concerns about energy rationing and a hit to industrial activity – in sharp contrast to markets pricing 2+ hikes in the next 6 months. This is consistent across the BoE’s policy rules (Figure 6) and the NiGEM results (Figure 5). We take more signal from the policy rules, as they are likely to be more representative of the central bank’s response function and because the analysis embeds our inflation and growth projections. These account for potential non-linear impacts, the UK economy’s starting point, and the unique transmission mechanism of higher energy prices to UK households via the Ofgem price cap methodology. We present the rest of the BoE’s policy rules and details on the specifications in the appendix. In line with this, we see scope for the BoE to deliver policy tightening this year (Figure 6). In the more benign scenarios (1 and 2), where the policy rules suggest fewer than two hikes, we think the central bank would prefer to look through the shock, opting to keep rates on hold at 3.75%. Instead, it would rely on the already restrictive nature of policy, the removal of its easing bias, and the weak starting point of the economy to limit second-round effects. In scenarios 3 and 4, we would expect rate hikes in 2026 but to a lesser extent than the policy rules imply due to recent rhetoric from MPC members. In the former (our working base case), we anticipate two back-to-back rate hikes, in June and July, for an end-2026 rate of 4.25%, following updated projections and guidance in April

Macroeconomic fundamentals and monetary policy: Bank Negara Malaysia held the overnight policy rate at 2.75% earlier this month, while acknowledging that Malaysia is facing the oil-shock risk from a position of strength. Indeed, the economy expanded 5.2% in 2025, its fastest pace in three years, with January industrial production surprising at 5.9% y/y growth (consensus expectation: 5.0%), supported by strong manufacturing performance in the computers and electronics sector. As a net-energy exporter with decent oil reserves, we think Malaysia is likely to remain relatively insulated from the oil shock (see FX: Asia’s sensitivity to supply-driven energy shocks, dated 11 March). The trade balance will also likely be cushioned by the higher value of energy exports. Meanwhile, headline inflation remained benign at 1.4% y/y in February. Given Malaysia’s better position to face the oil shock, the central bank may remain confident in keeping policy rates on hold here. Optimisation of hyperparameters with a surrogate model: To find the optimal hyperparameters in a more efficient way than a comprehensive grid search or random search, we use a surrogate model approach. This involves estimating a regression tree that is trained on the Sharpe ratios and parameters in the initial grid search. This model is then queried to find which parameters should, in theory, maximise the Sharpe ratio. Rince and repeat: The optimal hyperparameters suggested by the surrogate model are used in the next round of grid searching. We then redefine the hyperparameters by constructing a low–center–high interval around each suggested hyperparameter value, using ± half-sigma as the bounds. The result of this additional grid searching is added into the regression tree surrogate model to improve its fit. This process is repeated three times, each iteration refining the parameters akin to gradient descent. records.text: Beyond the metrics of credit stress, sector concentration in Software and other asset-light, higher value service industries has been in focus given the heightened attention on the potential for disruptive artificial intelligence (AI) new entrants. While Software loans represent roughly 20% of all BDC loans (per PitchBook data as of September 2025), our review of portfolio-level data does not yet show growing signs of impairment in this sector. That said, public loan price action in the sector has been fairly punitive already and historically tends to lead rating degradation and subsequent defaults. While the “ AI-disruption” thesis is inherently difficult to falsify (at least in the near-term) and will likely continue to have staying power, we believe underwriting practices and business specifics should matter more for senior lending. This should also drive wider dispersion within the sector, moving beyond simple beta exposure. Marks: Not obviously “wrong,” but likely to keep trending A central worry in recent months has also been whether BDC marks are stale, or misaligned across managers. The cross-manager data argues against the narrative: for loans with three or more borrowers, dispersion in portfolio marks has narrowed meaningfully, with the median differential now below $0.5 of par value and well below the prior peaks in 2022-23 (Exhibit 4). An inflationary shock can improve public finances through a ‘denominator effect’, but primarily when the shock appears on the demand side. External supply-side shocks – such as higher energy prices – tend to hurt the public purse despite a temporary lift in nominal growth (ECB, 2023). The current shock is therefore likely to worsen the UK’s fiscal position, with debt interest costs set to rise (Figure 7), while policy levers remain limited. Even if energy support measures are limited, the starting point from a fiscal perspective is less favourable. Higher spending on debt interest and automatic stabilisers is only somewhat balanced by greater revenues from windfall taxes on energy producers. Given it is our working base case, we analyse the pre-policy fiscal implications of scenario 3, embedding our growth, inflation and policy rate projections. We find that pre-policy, public-sector net borrowing (PSNB) is GBP3bn higher in FY2026/27, translating to a central government net cash requirement (CGNCR) of GBP141bn. This is consistent with price action since the outbreak of the Middle East crisis at end-February, with the 2s10s having already flattened more than 40bp. Further, we think Thailand’s fiscal concerns may rise, as fuel subsidies and fuel-export curbs are in place. Finally, gold coming under pressure amid global risk-off sentiment is also likely to weigh on the currency. Macroeconomic fundamentals and monetary policy: The Bank of Thailand delivered a surprise rate cut in February, citing structural impediments and intensified competition weighing on growth, while downside risks around inflation increased their need to help anchor medium-term inflation at higher levels. Low prevailing inflation (−0.88% y/y in February) and fuel subsidies could cushion a spike in prices, but the negative effect of the Middle East conflict on tourism and weakening trade sentiment is likely to weigh on growth. Further, Thailand is close to reaching its fiscal constraints on maintaining fuel subsidies. The Oil Fuel Fund is incurring about THB1bn/day at a time when the country’s fiscal deficit is projected to be at 68.2%, near the 70% limit. BDCs represent a relatively small slice of traditional private credit assets, with roughly $500 billion in total portfolio value, largely in the form of first- and second-lien loans. Despite their smaller size, they remain in focus for two reasons. First, they can provide a clearer picture of retail investor flows. Second, they can provide a more visible data trail given the requirement for quarterly public SEC filings on portfolios. Some stress, but not for all Based on available data through the fourth quarter (covering roughly 75% of total fair value in BDC portfolios), the share of loans trading below $80 has inched upwards to 2%, but remains below the 3% average since 2015 (Exhibit 1). At the same time, cross-manager dispersion in distressed exposure has drifted down from the 2023 highs, suggesting some consolidation in lower priced loans across managers but no signs of a “catch down” for the broader industry (again, Exhibit 1). Payment-in-kind (PIK) metrics also point to some rising stress, but the signal remains mixed. We have put our FX forecasts under review. For GBPUSD, we see it as a downside risk to our already bearish base case. The energy shock is bearish for the GBP through three channels. ▪ The UK is an energy importer with net energy imports worth 1% of GDP in 2024. ▪ It is negative for UK growth. Should oil prices stay above USD100/bbl for three to six months, we estimate it would subtract 0.7% from GDP, raising the risk of recession (see Europe: Vulnerable to Middle East shock, dated 6 March). The growth shock to the UK is primarily driven by the shock to private consumption. records.text: rbinger of an economic downturn (as history might suggest), in our view. ▪ Sturdy earnings growth: We look for a 0.4% rise in average hourly earnings and a steady y/y pace at 3.8%. We doubt that the Fed is concerned about wage pressures at current levels, particularly with productivity running at a solid clip (Figure 9), but this could change if unemployment were to start declining again. ▪ Unemployment rate is key, likely stable at 4.4%: We look for a 4.4% unemployment rate, matching the prior month. The February report reinforced our view that new labor supply in the job market is constrained. Not only was the participation rate revised lower by 0.4pp in January, but it fell again in February. Had it held steady in February, the jobless rate would have printed at 4.5%, not 4.4%. Echoes of Liberation Day for the long end: The impact on rates from the conflict is exhibiting parallels to post- Liberation Day price action, meaning long-end yields could see a self-reinforcing rise (see US rates: Echoes of Liberation Day, dated 6 March). Two factors make long- end yields vulnerable now. First, markets have heavily discounted risks of wider deficits after the conflict escalated. Term premiums are still close to the bottom of their recent ranges. Second, long-end swap spreads are falling sharply, which entails the selling of Treasuries which could be self-propagating. The V-shape rises in Treasury yields during the Liberation Day’s “Sell America” episode and Covid’s “dash for cash” were paired with decreasing liquidity and upward pressure on financing costs as dealers became more constrained. Consequently, rising repo rollover and margin risks forced a deleveraging in swap spread trades and cheapened them further, pushing long-end Treasury yields higher in parallel. Swap spreads currently face a triple threat: equity drawdown increasing swap receiving flows, potential for destabilizing inflation expectations, and wider deficits to fund the conflict pushing term premiums higher. At the same time, we don’t expect the fiscal response to be as forceful as in 2022, given the limited fiscal space. This would imply that the fiscal cushion to growth would likely be lower than before and could prevent embedded inflation (even if it doesn’t limit the peak in inflation). What are the conditions for a hike? The BoE noted that “a larger or more protracted shock which risked greater second-round effects in wage and price setting, would require a more restrictive policy stance i.e. opening the door to hikes”. Under current energy futures (with oil prices close to $100 but moving gradually to $80 by year end), we estimate that inflation can rise from current levels to ~3.5% in H2. Higher inflation is likely to squeeze real incomes and consumer caution is likely to rise amid another price shock/ weak labour market and weigh on growth by ~40bps. In this scenario risk of no cuts materializing in 2026 is likely to rise, with cuts likely resuming in 2027. Moreover, insurance hikes (one or two) can’t be ruled out mid-year, especially if the shock looks prolonged, inflation/wage expectations move higher and labour market doesn’t worsen. records.text: United Kingdom Outlook Correctly cautious Inflation was stable in February but inflation expectations data highlight the upward pressure to come. Retail sales, consumer confidence and PMIs all point to weakness in activity. Against this backdrop, the MPC communication has been cautious. • Headline CPI inflation in February printed at 3.0%, unchanged from January. Incorporating• this and the latest pump prices adds 0.05pp to our forecast for 2026, but leaves 2027 unchanged. Looking ahead, large increases in inflation expectations in March highlight the upside risks to our medium-term outlook. • Flash PMIs for March fell in both services and manufacturing, with a similarly weak signal• coming from consumer confidence. Retail sales for February contracted 0.4%. We maintain our view that real GDP growth in Q1 will now be 0.2% q/q. Next week we get the final estimate for Q4 25. • Bank of England speakers retained a non-committal and cautious tone against an uncertain• backdrop. All acknowledge that the economic context in which the current shock hits is different to 2021/22, but there are a range of views expressed about how to balance risks of de-anchoring inflation expectations versus demand destruction. Inflation was on track, before it was derailed February CPI data this week showed headline inflation remaining at 3.0% y/y. Core CPI reaccelerated 0.1pp to 3.2% as easing services price inflation (-0.1pp to 4.2%) was offset by an expected increase in core goods (+0.5pp to 1.3%).

records.text: US Outlook Out hot at the front end The front end continued to price in the possibility of hikes this week, even amid Fed communications emphasizing risks of more delayed cuts. With available measures showing limited fallout of high oil prices on inflation expectations, we continue to think that the move is premature. • With events in the Middle East intensifying risks of more prolonged supply disruptions to oil• and other key commodities, markets continue to boost the weighting of Fed hike scenarios. Although much depends on the duration of the shock, we think that markets are misinterpreting the Fed's likely reaction function. We believe risks of an extended hold are much higher, and we can't rule out deeper cuts. • The week's limited dataflow provides little indication that the Fed will deviate from its hold.• Neither longer-term market-implied inflation expectations nor five-to-ten year Michigan Survey inflation expectations indicate that households are questioning the credibility of the Fed's 2% inflation target. Next week's payroll and retail sales data should help assess demand fallout. • Recent data have fueled optimism that the US has already enter a phase of structurally faster• productivity growth, driven by AI and surging tech investment. We think recent strength largely reflects cyclical normalization rather than a clear productivity regime shift. The question then becomes whether this relationship should mean revert or is this conflict an entirely new paradigm for Euro credit? 2022 is a good example of a conflict and oil price surge meaningfully changing this relationship and indeed looking at the relative perfor- mance of US versus EUR credit during that time shows Europe lagging sharply: US IG spreads traded in a 45bp range of 134-180bp during those 6 months versus EUR IG spreads traded at nearly double the range or 94bp (142-236bp). Thus, the spread differential hit -60bp in June and October 2022 (or more than 10x the current -5.4bp we note above). Com- paring the commodity market reaction function, Brent has spiked averaging $96.5/bbl since the start of the Middle East conflict, just 11% lower than the average price during those 6 months in 2022. However, while oil is a global market and thus a headwind for both markets, natural gas is more local and thus an additional vulnerability for Europe (importer vs the US is an exporter). Gas has not repriced to 2022 levels yet (the current ~$18/mmbtu is still 54% below the 6m average in 2022) and thus any further volatility there would likely extend Europe’s underperformance. Thus, looking at further Europe underperformance in both cash or synthetics (or USD yankee banks as we note below) as a hedge into what may be another volatile weekend seems appropriate to us.

Morgan Meanwhile in inflation markets, front-end breakevens narrowed this week, largely on optimism around a near-term resolution. Real yields have also increased significantly in recent weeks, with synthetic front-end forward real yields rising to their highest levels in nearly a year. We think front-end real yields offer asymmetric risk-reward, with a near- term resolution likely to unwind hawkish Fed pricing, whereas a prolonged conflict could lead to greater recession fears. We also think breakevens have room to widen further as oil prices move higher, the macro backdrop remains supportive, and with valuations appearing cheap. However, we remain neutral on breakevens, as the duration of the conflict and supply shortages remain uncertain and higher oil prices risk both softer growth and depressed risk sentiment (see TIPS). Sectoral performance showed divergence, with the main lift coming from jumps in certain policy tailwinds sectors and raw materials sector. Our JPY view has been bearish since Sanae Takaichi was elected Prime Minister and was reinforced after the Liberal Democratic Party achieved a landslide majority in February’s lower-house election. We expect the Takaichi administration to proceed with expansionary fiscal policies, which adds inflationary pressure domestically, with limited upside to growth. As a result, this puts steepening pressure on JGBs as markets grow concerned that the Bank of Japan may fall behind on inflation, and so we think that the JPY will have to weaken to act as a release valve. We think this negative cycle will be reinforced by the global energy price shock. Japan is a net importer of energy and has the largest energy trade deficit in the G10 complex (as a percentage of GDP). Higher energy-import costs are negative for growth but at the same time contribute to higher inflation. For the BoJ, to the extent that this means it must balance the adverse impact of elevated energy prices on the economy, it could increase the risks of the BoJ falling behind the curve on inflation. Need for imports GCC countries have been engaged in diversifying their econ- omies, pursuing different "vision" agendas. While the non-oil GDP share has increased over time, the hydrocarbon sector still represents about a third of GDP. The journey toward a diversified economy and satisfaction of domestic demand requires large amounts of imports (Figure 1). The GCC area accounts for approximately 3% of global imports, worth over US700bn on average between 2022 and 2024 (Figure 2). Machinery is at the top of the list with more than US$190bn imported on average, linked to the aforementioned strong push toward diversification and large capex projects. Similar- ly, transport goods are substantial, accounting for almost 4% of global exports of this category. The area is also a key mar- ket for precious metals, with imports above 12% of global flows. Notably, food imports are also large due to the chal- lenging climate and are needed to satisfy both the local popu- lation and international visitors. Flows via Yanbu—its main Red Sea export terminal—have risen from 750 kbd to 4.3 mbd, with another 0.5 mbd of rerouting capacity available (Figure 3). To support this shift, the country has positioned nearly 50 VLCCs in the Red Sea, many currently waiting to load—creating a highly visible, concentrated fleet exposure. • The gateway is the Bab el-Mandeb, a narrow strait at the southern end of the Red Sea, effectively the main outlet for Red Sea exports headed to Asian markets. When this confidence is very high, it has been shown to be a leading signal that the bubble may be about to burst, or at least pause its expansion. As a result, we think the LPPLS Confidence Indicator (CI) can be used to inform trading decisions based on where an asset lies between the no-bubble, early-stage bubble or late-stage bubble categories (Figure 2). The challenge of fitting the model: We extend the current literature by implementing hyperparameterisation of the model based on the profitability of a trading model (rather than based on a statistical fit). We use a surrogate regression tree model to reduce the computation time of the calibration from several weeks of run-time to several days. In less technical terms, we calibrated the specification of the model for gold using a second model to predict which specification would deliver the best trading performance. Gold appears in a no bubble stage: The LPPLS Confidence Indicator, which currently stands at 0, signals that gold is in the “no-bubble” phase of the cycle, leading the model to favor a long position. Since the start of March 2026, a sell-off in gold has driven the LPPLS confidence score down from an extreme value of 1 to the present 0, indicating that the bubble has likely burst. For now, the pace of investment and capital deepening seems much too slow to drive sustained acceleration. Cart before horse To our surprise, markets continued to price in hike scenarios this week, with fed funds futures implying roughly 25% odds of a 25bp increase by December 2025 ( Figure 1). This appears to reflect growing weight on tail scenarios in which inflation pressures force the Fed to deliver a few precautionary hikes before resuming cuts. We acknowledge that recent supply shocks—particularly in energy and other commodities— have raised the probability of such outcomes. Still, we doubt this represents the most likely risk scenario. As we argued last week, the Fed is unlikely to hike absent evidence of a sustained acceleration in core prices, such as a material rise in longer‑term inflation expectations or a persistent inflationary shock that risks unmooring them. Available indicators point in the opposite direction: market‑implied 5-10yr expectations have drifted lower, while the University of Michigan’s 5-10yr measure held steady at 3.2% (consensus 3.5%) in the final March release. Nor do we think the FOMC sees parallels with 2021–22, which reflected a unique mix of severely constrained supply chains and surging goods demand that seems at odds with the present situation. 27 March 2026 11 FICC Research Economics 27 March 2026 Jonathan Millar +1 212 526 4876 jonathan.millar@barclays.c

Income returns have been remarkably stable, though growth rates appear to have fallen over time. Capital returns from property price changes have been more volatile, generally as a reaction to the economic cycle, but against a broader backdrop of broadly declining real yields. This difference in the behavior of the sources of return makes intuitive sense. CRE income generally comes from long-term contractual leases and, in many cases, with CPI escalators. Capital returns are informed more so by the market’s assessment of the valuation multiples that should be assigned to cashflows. Typical of equity instruments, a slowdown in growth leads to price declines (recessions pushing capital returns into negative territory) and reflationary periods lead to positive capital returns. records.text: PRECIOUS METALS VIEW After correcting sharply in early February following President Donald Trump’s nomination of Kevin Warsh as the next Fed chair, gold rallied to c.USD625/oz through the month, spurred by strong physical gold interest. Central banks continue to accumulate gold holdings apace, most notably in Europe, whilst bar and coin investors surged back to the market last month, particularly in Asia, providing significant price support. Typically, physical gold buying, whether direct uptake of gold bars and coins, or indirectly via physically backed exchange-traded funds (ETFs), tends to be relatively sticky – i.e. limited selling in a correction. However, the USD’s sharp rebound in early March, following the start of ‘Operation Epic Fury’ in the Arabian Gulf and the subsequent oil price spike, saw gold retreat towards key support levels of c.USD5,000/oz. by mid-March. As well as USD strength, gold has had to contend with a risk-off driven correction in equity markets, prompting gold selling to meet equity-margin calls. However, such selling is also likely to be muted in terms of impact, in our view, particularly as speculative net futures’ length in CME gold futures has generally been on a declining trend over the last year. Given continued physical market interest, current heightened geopolitical risks and macro-economic uncertainty, we reiterate our view that a ‘buy the dip’ approach is the right strategy for the yellow metal.
