This therefore makes the currency one of the the best-positioned in EM, in our view. Higher oil prices are also advantageous for Brazil relative to peers, as the country is a net exporter of crude. The consequent (minor) improvement in the trade balance gives the BRL modest additional support. In monetary policy, the BCB has initiated an easing cycle, but we think it will proceed cautiously given still-robust domestic activity and the upside inflation risk from higher oil prices. The future major purchase intentions series dropped 6pt to -18; current savings opportunities rose 6pt to 27 but future saving opportunities fell 9pt to 21. This constellation, to us, suggests consumers are reining in spending and trying to boost savings to smooth through the cost shock. On the price front, future price expectations rose 9pt, to 98, which is the highest since April 2025. A similar story was painted by the March flash PMI (for full details of our interpretation of the data, see A hint of stagflation, 24 March). The composite index fell 2.7pt from February, to 51.0. For the past two weeks, the price of crude oil has been choppy largely within a $100 to 110/bbl range, despite the continued lack of product flowing through the Strait of Hormuz. Futures markets continue to price Brent crude to return to $85/bbl by the end of the year, which remains the reference point for our current assessment of the econom- ic outlook. But the longer the oil disruption goes on, the more the risks rise—albeit likely more in energy-exposed countries elsewhere than in the US. On Thursday our commodity analysts characterized the current environment as shifting from a “flow shock” to a “stock depletion problem.” Tankers departing the Persian Gulf take 10-20 days to reach Asia, 20-35 days to reach Europe and Africa, and 35-45 days to reach the US Gulf Coast. That means physical shortages are felt at different times in different regions, with the US last in line.

If redemptions start to pressure BDC liquidity, we think that private credit valuations could shift from a “mark to model” framework towards a more traditional mark-to-market approach driven by broadly syndicated loan market comps, amplified by higher-frequency marks on semi-liquid products, public/private BDC arbitrage, and more prudent collateral revaluation by banks offering leverage. Historically, the leveraged loan market has been a key input to private market valuations, and we believe that gauging potential mark to market impacts starts with historical context on B- and CCC-rated loans. Empirically, low single B (B3/B-) loan exposure traded to $90 during the 2022-23 Fed tightening moment, $80 briefly during COVID, mid-$80s during the high-yield shale crisis, and mid-$50s during the GFC. These data points, in our view, are possible estimates for how mark to market portfolio pricing could evolve on private credit portfolios – albeit with potentially less severity and a lag – depending on the timing of higher defaults due to AI-disruption risks. records.text: CORPORATE MARKETS MONTHLY Or, cet ancrage des anticipations d’inflation ne peut plus être considéré comme acquis. Le choc inflationniste lié à l'énergie est le quatrième choc de prix consécutif en cinq ans, venant après la réouverture du marché post- pandémie, l'invasion de l'Ukraine par la Russie et aux annonces de tarifs douaniers du « Liberation Day » de 2025. « Wait and See » : Cela étant dit, certaines différences fondamentales dans la situation macroéconomique rendent l'ampleur de la réponse de la politique monétaire probablement différente de la période post-2022. Premièrement, l'inflation était alors élevée et en hausse, alors qu'elle est désormais stable ou en déclin dans la plupart des régions. Deuxièmement, les marchés du travail sont tendus, mais pas en surchauffe comme en 2022. Troisièmement, les taux directeurs sont déjà proches de la neutralité, alors que le point de départ en 2022 était une politique monétaire profondément accommodante. Enfin, avec des rendements sensiblement plus élevés, la politique budgétaire a moins de marge pour amortir l'économie cette fois-ci, ce qui rend plus probable un affaiblissement de la demande en réponse à la hausse des prix de l'énergie. Néanmoins, la période de 2022 nous enseigne que des réponses lentes peuvent amplifier le problème, alimentant le risque d’un virage de politique monétaire plus brutal plus tard. En conséquence, nous pensons que les banques centrales seront probablement plus promptes à réagir cette fois-ci. Nous

records.text: patterns emerge: Directional rates move. EM rates tend to rise, driven by concerns about inflation, currency depreciation, and potential monetary policy tightening. This is particularly true for countries with high oil import bills (notably in CEEMEA and Asia), as they face increased pressure on their trade balances and currencies. After oil prices peak, the reversal of the sell-off in EM rates tends to be limited, with Latam being the exception (Figures 17– 20). Curve. The short-end rates curve tends to steepen (1s5s), while the long-end curve flattens (5s10s). This indicates market expectations for higher inflation and potential interest rate hikes by central banks, which may have a negative impact on economic growth in the future. This is in line with our findings in FX and energy Q&A: Strait answers, dated 12 March, where we also explored the impact on FX more broadly. The shape of the curve also depends on the peak oil price and timeframe of the oil shock. The initial move higher in oil prices causes 1s5s steepening with 5s10s flattening. As oil prices go much higher (typically above USD100/bbl) or stay high for a long time, 1s2s keeps on steepening, but 2s5s starts to echo the 5s10s flattening as the market starts to factor in a greater probability of a growth shock. Asset swap spread (ASW). The ASW (bond yield minus swap rate) tends to tighten with bonds outperforming swaps. Les courbes de taux devraient continuer à s'aplatir, les taux à court terme restant sous pression, tandis que les maturités à long terme reflèteront des attentes de croissance plus faibles. Gestion des risques pour les entreprises : Sans surprise, les tendances en matière de gestion des risques au cours des dernières semaines ont été façonnées par le conflit au Moyen-Orient et l’évolution des prix qui en a découlé sur les marchés financiers. La gestion de la liquidité et les appels de marge ont été au centre des préoccupations des entreprises négociant sur les marchés financiers, beaucoup prenant des mesures proactives pour renforcer leur liquidité en prévision de nouvelles hausses des prix de l'énergie. Alors que certains avaient préfinancé, d'autres ont exploré des solutions telles que les repos ou les swaps de liquidité. We recently outlined the potential impacts of four energy price scenarios on the eurozone economy and on the European Central Bank (see Europe: Energy shock prompts market paradigm shift, dated March 20). Here we replicate that approach for the UK, analysing the possible impact of four scenarios on inflation, BoE policy, rates, FX and equities. This envisioned inflation returning to target, the Bank of England delivering further rate cuts, and fiscal policy risks being contained. This view has been upended by the conflict. We anticipate energy prices to add 0.4% to head- line inflation in the upcoming March report, which would generate the largest monthly gain since 2022. The impact of higher energy prices varies across countries, and some governments have stepped in to limit the pass- through to retail prices. In next week’s report, Euro area HICP inflation is expected to jump from 1.9% to 2.5%oya, but core is likely to ease to 2.2%oya (reversing the Olympics-related February rise). A more substantial headline CPI impact is expected in Poland (+1%ppt to 3.3%yoa) whereas Korea’s wholesale price cap should keep inflation close to 2%. For central banks, a main concern is whether the shock will spill over into higher core inflation. Transportation services are an obvious place to look for large price increases in com- ing months. March is likely too soon to expect a broad impact, but our forecasts incorporate a modest firming in core next quarter as the surge in a broad range of commodity pric- es points to renewed upward pressure on global goods prices, including food.

How much energy imports from Gulf We begin by gauging China’s exposure to the disruption in the Strait of Hormuz. Against the backdrop of the US‑China tariff conflict that began in the first Trump administration, China has steadily pursued diversification of its key external supplies. This effort predates the current crisis and accelerat- ed after the Russia‑Ukraine war, when commodity stockpiling expanded on national‑security grounds. The “friend‑shoring” approach for essential commodities aims to hard‑wire redun- dancy and optionality into supply chains: diversifying import origins, co‑locating production with trusted partners, and reinforcing domestic “last‑mile” capabilities. Including flows from Iran, the Middle East suppliers account for roughly 55% of China’s crude imports, with the rest com- ing from Russia, Malaysia and others (Figure 1). This diversi- fied import matrix mitigates some physical disruption risk, but the drag would become more pronounced if the current conflict endures. Complete report: US Economic Weekly: Adding deficits to the wall of worry 27 March 2026 Deficit risks have shifted higher Markets have responded quickly to the inflation risks posed by the ongoing Iran war. As a result, market participants are pricing in hikes by the Fed this year, and the yield curve has flattened (Exhibit 1). Another risk the war poses that markets may not yet be fully pricing in is a deterioration in the deficit trajectory. The war and tariff refunds pose meaningful upside risk to our deficit forecasts, which are currently $1.875tn (5.8% of GDP) in FY 26 and $1.925tn (5.7% of GDP) in FY 27. Should the trajectory of deficits shift materially higher, fiscal concerns could re-emerge. That would likely put upward pressure on long-end rates and raise borrowing costs for businesses and households. To date, US retail gasoline prices have already increased to close to $4/gallon, but our commodity colleagues see a risk of that exceeding $5 if the Strait remains effectively closed by mid-April. In February, the BEA estimated that households spent about $420bn on energy goods at an annualized pace, mostly gasoline, and since then prices are a little less than 30% above their 2025 average. That equates to around $115bn in additional annualized outlays on energy, over half of our estimate of the full-year reduction in personal taxes from OBBBA in 2026. In other words, the cost shock will be substantial if prices stay at least this high for an extend- ed period. Were gasoline prices to rise to $5/gal, it would put them back near the highs of the past couple of decades. On an inflation-adjusted basis, prices exceeded $5/gal briefly during the start of the Russia-Ukraine war in 2022 and in the lead up to the Great Recession, as well as for a multi-year period following the Great Recession (Figure 1). The 14th FYP (2021) reiterated the Deng-era mantra that "peace and development remain the themes of the times" but, reflecting the rising challenges to globalization, added that “the world has entered a new period of turbulence and trans- formation, where unilateralism, protectionism, and hegemony pose threats to world peace and development.” As discussed earlier, in this plan period China shifted to increased com- modity stockpiling and redirected both exports and imports away from developed to emerging markets in Asia, Africa, and Latin America. The 15th FYP entirely omits any reference to “peace and development” as the “theme of the times.” Instead, it assesses deglobalization and geopolitical rivalry to be the primary drivers of an increasingly uncertain and unstable future global economy. This change, in our view, elevates national security to a cen- tral and over-arching principle for economic policies in the 15th FYP. In the details, this is reflected in accelerated and ambitious targets for self-sufficiency and modernization in core technologies, increased resiliency of supply chains through onshoring and friendshoring, advancing military modernization, and expanding strategic reserves of food and energy. The bottom line Argentina has the raw materials and, for now, the policy framework to build a manufacturing sector grounded in genu- ine comparative advantage. The real exchange rate isn’t hold- ing back competitive sectors, and the current account deficit remains manageable— unlike during Macri’s early years or the Convertibility era. But the formal employment question imposes a binding con- straint on the speed of liberalization that no exchange rate can dissolve. The sectors that can compete globally are, by struc- ture, not the sectors that currently employ the most formal manufacturing workers. Bridging that gap requires time, tar- geted retraining investment, and a liberalization timeline long enough for competitive job creation to partially offset protect- ed-sector contraction. In our view, the opening-up process should still move ahead, even if at the expense of a higher unemployment rate in the short-run, to avoid the country being condemned to permanently low productivity and ane- mic per capita growth. The impact on private credit is expected to be limited under the 2-month disruption scenario, assuming oil prices remain below $100 for most of the quarter. In this scenario, YoY US real GDP forecasts through Q1 2027 would decline by 0.2-0.3%, and the Fed would likely hold rates instead of implementing two cuts in 2H 2026, which we do not think will have a significant impact on the asset class. However, an extended disruption scenario driving oil prices towards $150 could trigger a 1990s-style recession, with US growth falling -1.2% to -1.4% in H2 to 0.2% and 0.5% in Q3 and Q4'26. We quantified the share of private credit portfolios with higher exposure to a prolonged Middle East escalation and found that ~11% of private credit portfolios are lower rated and at higher risk of prolonged disruption to oil. For global LL and HY portfolios, the exposures are 6-7% and ~5%, respectively. As private BDC's face redemptions, how do you expect valuations to respond? BDCs account for one-third of invested private credit assets ($0.5tn out of ~$1.5tn), with two-thirds of BDC's in private non-traded vehicles, the portion of the universe which carries redemption risk. In the medium term, the TWD will probably underperform peers because of efficient current account recycling via overseas direct and outbound investment and life insurers unwinding FX hedges. Macroeconomic fundamentals and monetary policy: The CBC kept the policy rate on hold at 2% at its March meeting (see Taiwan: CBC delivers a cautious tone amidst high uncertainty, dated 20 March), while raising both its GDP and CPI forecasts. We believe the CBC remains cautious to keep the door open for rate hikes amid high uncertainty. Considering Taiwan’s robust growth backdrop, albeit K-shaped, the CBC will probably not hesitate to raise policy rate if it sees any sign of a rise in inflation expectations, in our view. While our base case remains that the CBC will hold the policy rate steady at 2% until end-2027, we think a prolonged Middle East conflict could trigger rate hikes.

records.text: Yes, markets are pricing higher inflation and tighter monetary policy than five weeks ago. But this is not evidence of mispriced fundamentals. Instead, it is a simple reflection of the market’s expectation of a quick resolution to the war. In other words, the expectation that the shock will be temporary and limited in size, with a temporary increase in inflation that would force the Fed to remain on hold and it would not be persistent enough to create significant destruction of economic activity. Markets might be overly optimistic about the outcome of the war. But the pricing is consistent with the consensus view that the war will be relatively short-lived and eventually energy prices will start to normalize before the end of the spring.

Political and policy responses Brazil’s response to global fuel price shocks has historically alternated between price controls, tax cuts, targeted subsidies, and negotiated solutions. This time, the government’s reac- tion has been swift and multifaceted, reflecting both the urgency of the external shock and the heightened political stakes of an election year. In contrast to the prior week, the government shifted from a proposed temporary regional V AT (ICMS) reduction on imported diesel—which faced legal and political hurdles—to a joint federal-state subsidy of 1.20 reais per liter. While this aims to ease implementation and avoid fiscal responsibility law constraints, resistance from some states remains, especially over revenue losses and the techni- calities of subsidy allocation. records.text: d card The confluence of the Vaca Muerta energy buildout and the critical minerals investment wave creates a potentially trans- formative channel for Argentine manufacturing that extends well beyond the extractive sectors themselves. Argentina’s industrial base has long suffered from an energy cost disad- vantage: decades of price distortions, underinvestment in gen- eration and transmission, and periodic rationing imposed a de facto tax on energy-intensive manufacturing subsectors — petrochemicals, steel, aluminum, glass, ceramics, and food processing — that eroded their international competitiveness. The normalization of energy tariffs under the current adminis- tration, combined with the rapid scaling of Vaca Muerta's nat- ural gas output is closing that cost gap. If sustained, cheaper and more reliable energy supply could deliver a structural reduction in unit production costs across the industrial matrix, enabling subsectors that have historically survived only behind tariff walls to approach cost structures consistent with export viability. Inflation review Headline CPI was flat in February at 3.0%, in line with consensus and BoE’s forecast. Core inflation rose from 3.1% to 3.2%, above consensus of 3.1% and 20bps above the BoE’s forecast. Services inflation fell from 4.4% to 4.3%, above consensus of 4.2% and 20bps above the BoE’s forecast. Energy and food inflation fell. Underlying services inflation fell more with BoE’s services excluding indexed and volatile components, rents and foreign holidays' falling from 4.3% to 4.1%. records.text: Global Economic Weekly | 27 March 2026 15 LNG capex potential seems greatest for AU We see Australia as best positioned, should the recent step-up in LNG prices prove durable and catalyzes a capex upcycle. Compared to Malaysia and especially Indonesia, Australia’s gas fields are at an earlier stage of maturity, while its LNG infrastructure is larger and more integrated. These structural advantages allow incremental capex to be deployed more efficiently, supporting asset life extension and helping to preserve export capacity over time. Coal: Quality premium may benefit AU more vs. ID Indonesia and Australia were the world’s largest exporters in 2024, supplying 30% and 26% of global coal export volume respectively (Exhibit 6). Australia mainly exports higher quality 5,500–6,000 kcal/kg coal. On the other hand, Indonesia coal exports are predominately lower quality grades, with 4,200 kcal/kg the most common. As such, unit export price for Australia is twice that of Indonesia (Exhibit 7). Between the two, we think that Australia could see greater support from price premiums on its higher quality coal, which tend to widen under tight market conditions. Our commodity analysts highlighted that quality differentials are likely to widen under tight LNG market conditions, as major buyers of Qatari LNG, such as Japan and South Korea, turn to the coal market and bid up higher-grade material. The Tech sector has minimal direct revenue exposure to the Mid- dle East, but the confluence of supply chain risk, energy cost inflation, and a broader risk-off sentiment represents a meaningful incremental headwind to monitor as the conflict evolves. The risk assessment at the April meeting will consider all the information and this can move significantly with the fluid sit- uation in Iran. How the latter evolves and how it affects ener- gy markets may be particularly important for the ECB’s over- all risk assessment. Assuming there is no quick resolution, the ECB staff has charted a hawkish baseline and risk assessment via the two scenarios. This should bias the ECB to moving. records.text: Sustained Strait closure raises risks of a more disruptive macro shock • Western European central banks now expected to hike next quarter ... • … while FOMC patience creates space for a diversified EM CB response • Next week: US jobs up (75k); global PMI off; Euro area HICP up 2.5%oya Time is on my side, no it isn’t As a resolution to the Middle East conflict is nowhere in sight, its macroeconomic imprint is set to build. It is too early to see its effects in activity or inflation readings: Current-quarter growth projections hold firm and global core CPI inflation looks to be tracking close to the 3%ar it has held for more than two years. But early signs of a coming stagflationary tilt are evident in the March surveys. Business output expectations and consumer confidence have slipped, alongside expectations of higher near-term inflation. Next week’s key March releases should deliver solid growth readings – with an anticipated 75k rise in US employment and a dip in the global manufacturing PMI output index to 52.5, a level consistent with a faster than 2% pace of factory output gain. But the momentum loss in the March PMIs is likely a sign of a growth drag that will build and we expect next week’s March CPI reports — led by a Euro area 0.7% HICP spike — to provide the first concrete indication that global CPI inflation is on track to rise towards 3.5%oya (Figure 1). records.text: Europe Economic Weekly | 27 March 2026 3 Weekly view Finger on the trigger The energy price shock is proving increasingly persistent. That is slowly leading to an outlook with less growth (already starting to show in soft data), more inflation (with next week’s March inflation print providing the initial look), and more hawkish central banks, at least in the near term. ECB: hawkish, but perhaps not quite so fast At this stage, we haven’t adjusted our European forecasts. We were hoping to get a little more visibility on the magnitude and longevity of the shock, but the wait is starting to become a long one. We are getting ready to make changes, but in the meantime, please have a look at our scenario analysis from two weeks ago ( Europe Economic Weekly: The ghosts from the past 06 March 2026. Under a more persistent shock to energy prices, increasingly likely, we would expect a couple of hikes this summer (in June and July), followed by cuts next year, to at least 1.5% sometime in mid-2027, with the exact timing depending on the energy profile. The ECB’s scenarios from last week would also chime with that view, we think. EM assets started the year well given a supportive global backdrop, but the shock of US/Israel strikes on Iran and Iranian retalia- tion by restricting the Straits of Hormuz and attacking GCC countries have reversed these gains, as it opens up tail risks of a global recession with high inflation. records.text: f inelastic demand may seem strong, it nonetheless may represent a lower bound on the likely drag consumers will face. Rising gasoline (or other energy) prices can have second-round effects on the prices of some items in core inflation (e.g., airfares, shipped goods). That said, most empirical studies for the US find small to negligible effects on core inflation from higher energy prices, whereas food prices are more responsive. This finding reflects not only a higher energy-intensity for agricultural production relative to other sectors, but also the fact that higher energy prices tend to be associated with higher fertilizer prices. Indeed, more than gasoline prices are being pushed up by the Middle East conflict. So too are prices for a range of other energy products and industrial supplies, from aluminum to urea for fertilizers, and sulfur and helium for high-tech manu- facturing processes. These could gradually leak into higher prices for consumer goods. We also do not build into our analysis any nonlinear effects that might arise at more elevat- ed crude oil prices. These would likely exacerbate the drag on consumers and boost the risk for a recession. Such nonlinear dynamics are associated with greater job loss and a sell-off in risky assets that would undo some of the post-pandemic wealth accumulation, not to mention damage sentiment. Additionally, the observation that gasoline and oil price spikes tend not to materially raise core inflation means those costs are assum

However, there are plausible cir- cumstances in which higher gasoline prices eat away much or all—or more—of the expected tax benefit this year. If real- ized, this situation would represent a downside risk to our current growth forecast for 2026. CLNs in B3E Over the last few years, CLNs have emerged as an important tool for transferring credit risk from bank portfolios to the private sector. However, banks have historically faced regulato- ry hurdles in obtaining capital relief from directly issued CLNs. The Basel III Endgame (B3E) proposal, published last Thursday, changes this landscape by introducing the Prepaid Credit Protection Arrangement (PCPA) framework. We believe this development will drive increased CLN issuance across various collateral types. For background, in 2023, the Federal Reserve clarified that banks may recognize capital relief using directly issued CLNs. Previously, banks could not automatically obtain capital relief from directly issued CLNs because these structures failed to meet the regulatory defi- nition of a synthetic securitization on two grounds: first, they do not include a guarantee or credit derivative; second, cash proceeds from the note sale are either deposited in a third-par- ty account or held on the bank’s balance sheet, neither of which qualifies as a credit risk mitigant under the prior regulatory framework. The US and Iran still appear too far apart to reach a compromise. The reported negotiations on the back of the deal the US put on the table this week are stuck, and escalation is more likely than not. Even if the war is over in a few weeks, it will take time to normalize flows and production of energy products and derivatives. The global economy has become less oil dependent over time, but if the war escalates and becomes protracted, non-linear consequences of much higher energy prices could be significant. At the risk of sounding like a broken record, the size and persistence of the shock is critical to determine its impact and how much of the stagflationary shock will be felt as an inflation and/or a growth shock. If Republicans can cobble together support for a party-line reconciliation bill that includes more defense spending, it would not surprise us to see other provisions included that would drive up the cost. For example, Congress could suspend the gas tax, an idea the President has supported, to provide some relief to households. This could add around $40bn/year to the deficit. Republicans in competitive midterm races would presumably push for more significant consumer relief. In thinking about the deficit impact of a potential reconciliation bill, any consumer relief is likely to be immediate due to the midterms. Based on prior supplemental bills for Ukraine and Israel, we think allocated increases in the defense budget would take time to fully be spent (Exhibit 3). That said, the costs of war could change significantly if the war continues for longer than expected and if it involves actual troops on the ground. For example, the costs of the Afghanistan, Iraq & Syria wars averaged more than $100bn/year in 2025$ (Exhibit 4). That would likely shift the narrative in markets back to concerns over debt levels in the US and could pressure the long end of the curve higher, given limited demand and the need to grow coupon issuance earlier than currently expected.

records.text: that the probability of an ECB hike in April is substantial, particularly if we get to that meeting with market pricing implying well above a 50% probability of that happening. That would give leverage to those pushing for an April hike. But market pricing can adjust with data. Sentiment and activity data can help with that in the run up to the next meeting. And ECB speak can help, too, if we hear more from those clearly not ready to rush. UK: moving the bar In the UK the bar for hikes is still higher than for the ECB, but not as high as a few weeks ago. Under current energy futures prices, risks of no cuts materializing in 2026 will rise. Insurance hikes (one or two) can’t be ruled out mid-year. We would still think April might be too early. But the context is also different from 2022. Hikes, if any, are likely to be modest unless we see much higher oil prices. If energy prices jump higher and that move is sustained (oil jumping above $130 in Q2/Q3) then the BoE can hike by 50-75bps, potentially as soon as April, if energy prices move to higher levels by then. The many shades of memory We were again reminded by Lagarde this week that this is not 2022 in many aspects. The shock is smaller and less persistent, at least so far (and especially on gas prices).

A focus on the tech sector is warranted given Taiwan’s energy exposure to the Middle East. We believe its LNG supply is secured through May and that the industry can flexibly man- age critical loads. Higher energy prices are likely, however, to reinforce tech pricing pressures in an industry where strong demand is generating broader supply constraints. This week’s 1.1% m/m rise in US non-fuel import prices was fueled by a record rise in tech products, a development consistent with the broader upward pressure on DRAM and other tech related prices. Absent an intensification of the supply shock, we think that the baseline path will lower global growth to a still solid pace. But two important resiliency tests will need to be passed in an environment in which oil prices remain at elevated levels through midyear. The first is that the immediate slide in busi- ness expectations does not extend in a way that short-circuits the tech spending boom and an expected labor market recou- pling. It is encouraging that March regional Fed surveys show a continued rise in employment expectations (Figure 4). Most metals have seen price levels breach 20- and 50-day moving averages, as further USD strength and global growth concerns weigh on the complex. The longer the disruption to Gulf shipping goes on, the greater the headwinds for most base metals, in our view. Only aluminium has seen significant upside. The Arabian Gulf is home to seven million tonnes of aluminium smelting capacity, accounting for c.8% of global capacity. With Gullf smelters starting to announce aluminium production cuts on dwindling alumina inventories, we still see further price upside for the metal. Spring wage negotiations start strong The agreed hike in base wages in the first round of Shunto negotiations averaged just over 3.8%, almost unchanged from last year’s level, marking the third consecutive year that base pay growth has surpassed 3%. Alongside adjustments for seniority-based payments, the rise in base pay leaves headline wage hikes at a little over 5%, only a touch lower than the average at this point in last year’s negotiations. As in previous years, results from the initial rounds of negoti- ations tend to be a little higher than the final agreements in the summer. The broadening in the later rounds of wage gains to smaller firms remains important given their large share in employment. In this context, recent sentiment data continues to look upbeat, particularly among SMEs, and last year’s negotiations suggested strong momentum in wage hikes. records.text: Looking at total returns—which will account for both the yield change and inflation accrual—we arrive at similar conclusions. We estimate that TIPS on an outright basis generated meaningfully (hypothetical) positive total returns in the 1970s and 1990— owing to a combination of lower TIPS yields and high underlying inflation (Exhibit 4). While TIPS returns were negative in 2022, in all instances returns to being long TIPS were superior to being long nominals from the start of the shock to the oil peak. However, after the peak the relative performance picture more closely resembles our earlier point on distinctions between the two 1970s energy shocks and the more recent ones (Exhibit 5). The more sustained inflation problems in the earlier episodes meant TIPS returns exceeded nominals in the period following the oil surge, whereas in 1990 and 2022 nominals were the better option once oil had peaked and inflation risks began to abate. During the 2022 commodity price shock episode, food and core CPI inflected higher with a six- to-nine month lag. Our sensitivity analysis shows that with a similar pass-through, core inflation could exceed the 4% upper bound this September and stay above-target through 2027 (Figure 6). KEY MESSAGES We explore the concept of modelling bubbles, starting with a focus on gold given its dramatic price rise over the last 12 months. We apply a model known as LPPLS to gold’s price action. This measures the extent to which price action fits a mathematical equation for a bubble. This is a computationally intensive model to fit. We calibrate the model based on maximising profitability of a trading strategy and using a surrogate regression tree model for the hyperparameterisation. Our framework results in three states: No bubble, early- stage bubble and late-stage bubble. After the recent decline, gold rests in the no bubble stage, suggesting scope for further gains. On the one hand, weak labor markets could keep recession risks elevated, but on the other hand, faster-than-expected productivity growth from AI could deliver better GDP growth. The recent Middle East conflict and the spike in energy prices naturally inject more risk into our outlook, given their potential to serve as a driver of inflation and a drag on consumer spending and economic growth. Indeed, our US econo- mists recently revised up their headline inflation forecast from 3.2% to 3.4% (Q4/Q4 2026) and lowered their Q2 GDP growth forecast from 2.0% q/q saar to 1.5%, but left their H2 forecast unchanged. But there are some important notes to these changes: 1) our economists note that energy price pass-through to core prices has been modest in recent decades and 2) while the downward revision to Q2 GDP is driven by lower real consumer spending expecta- tions, some of it is offset by an increase in productivity growth expectations due to AI. Against this base case view of the economy staying resilient, CRE income growth and prices could remain stable. But a more material slowdown in growth coupled with higher inflation expectations is not a good recipe for CRE broadly. Income growth can be durable for long- leased assets, and the ability for CRE landlords to pass-through inflation to tenants helps preserve this durability in an inflationary environment. records.text: Global Synthesis Extend... and hope for an end Four weeks into the Iran war, the Strait of Hormuz remains closed. Under the US threat of further escalation, negotiations have started through proxies, for which the deadline has been extended to 6 April. Markets now price a more protracted conflict while fresh data show the imprints of higher oil. Cracks, but not a crater for 2026... Preparing a quarterly outlook amid the ongoing developments is even more challenging than making predictions already is under more calm circumstances. In our Global Outlook publication Cracks, but not a crater this week, we still try. We argue that despite the sharp repricing of front-end rates curves, asset prices have so far reacted in a measured fashion, consistent with a conflict that will eventually fade in the coming weeks. We argue that, in our base case, the US-Iran conflict will remain more an inflation shock than a growth shock, allowing the world to still grow 3% this year, and that beneath the headlines, a largely acyclical investment cycle – driven not just by AI, but also by defense and energy-related spending – is gathering momentum. We agree that private credit in the US has real problems, especially in software, but view these as slow‑burn and non‑systemic. That equates to around $115bn in addi- tional annualized outlays on energy, over half of our estimate of the full-year reduction in personal taxes from OBBBA in 2026. In other words, the cost shock will be substantial if prices stay at least this high for an extended period. Were gasoline prices to rise to $5/gal, it would put them back near the highs of the past couple of decades. On an inflation- adjusted basis, prices exceeded $5/gal briefly during the start of the Russia-Ukraine war in 2022 and in the lead up to the Great Recession, as well as for a multi-year period following the Great Recession (Figure 1). The share of total consump- tion devoted to energy goods hasn’t changed that much over recent decades, so the increase in prices would likely push the energy goods share of consumption back to levels similar to then, unless perhaps households are able to economize on use, such as engaging in more remote work. records.text: 13 Sajjid Z Chinoy(91-22) 6157-3386 sajjid.z.chinoy@jpmorgan.com JPMorgan Chase Bank, N.A., Mumbai Branch Global Economic Research 27 March 2026 J P M O R G A N Is this 2020 or 2022? What complicates the current energy shock is an assessment of how large the growth shock will be. When energy prices spiked after the onset of the Russia-Ukraine conflict in 2022, the shock operated largely though higher prices, and an adverse terms-of-trade channel. There was never any concern about actual shortages of energy supply. This time could be different. With Asia sourcing more than 50% of its crude and more than a third of its gas via the Strait of Hormuz, the region faces a physical lack of availability of energy volumes if the Strait of Hormuz remains closed for a prolonged period. We define beta as the ratio of the peak-to-trough 2s10s move – measured from the average level in the month four months prior to the first hike, to the trough reached in the 12 months following – to the total tightening delivered. Betas range from over 150% in 1999 to just 13% in the most recent cycle (2021–23). We find that the average beta is around 80% for 2s10s and 66% for 10s30s; the lower beta on the latter reflects the longer end’s greater sensitivity to supply and term premium dynamics relative to rate expectations. We use these estimates to illustrate in Figure 10 the potential flattening implied under different rate hike To illustrate the range of potential outcomes in more depth, we segment historical hiking cycles into two groups based on their curve sensitivity: those that exhibited a higher beta and those with a lower beta (Figure 11). This gives us a range: for 75bp of hikes (our scenario 4), the implied 2s10s flattening spans roughly 70–160% depending on which regime prevails. Figure 12 then maps the same two groups in terms of total hikes against total curve flattening, to further illustrate the dispersion across cycles. The key takeaway is that we do not expect more than 100bp of hikes in any of our scenarios. Indeed, she stressed that the 2% infla- tion target “has proved its worth” as inflation expectations remained anchored during the 2022-23 high inflation period. Implicit in this discussion was a suggestion that old ways of “looking through” certain supply shocks—as was done ini- tially during the 2022-23 post-pandemic inflation—would also need to be reconsidered. So, too, she stated, would com- munications around underlying inflation and the measurement of shelter inflation. Despite not saying anything explicit about the current policy stance, markets have broadly interpreted recent BoC rhetoric as hawkish: market forwards are current- ly pricing over two hikes by year-end. We remain skeptical: while the inflation targeting framework did not preclude the sharp acceleration in inflation, its success during 2022-23 was that the BoC did not need to engineer a recession to bring inflation back down. But that was a period of rapid expansion as the economy reopened from COVID- era lockdowns and immigration was strong. Now the econo- my has been weakened by the US trade war and a sharp cur- tailing of immigration, and an oil supply shock appears poised to kick Canadian households and sectors outside of energy when they are already down. records.text: TIPS still work well as hedge in 60/40 portfolios So while TIPS might not be as attractive as an investment following the peak of an oil shock as in the runup, they have historically offered hedge value relative to nominals against equity selloffs in cost-push shocks (i.e. where growth is hit and inflation spikes). The more recent observations suggest that in a world of anchored inflation expectations TIPS excess value comes mostly from the mechanics of higher underlying inflation and perhaps a simultaneous response in inflation risk premia, some of which abates after oil peaks. Ideally, investors then should rotate into nominals as they cheapen relative to TIPS while the shock is ongoing. However, from a diversification perspective we do not find that 60/40 portfolios have fared meaningfully worse in vol-adjusted terms following the oil peak in prior shocks (Exhibit 6), or outside of supply shocks in general, reducing the opportunity cost of a preference for TIPS over nominals. Why this time is different, and why TIPS can work from here The findings from past episodes stand somewhat at odds with pricing during the current shock, where long-end TIPS have underperformed despite the pickup in inflation. As discussed above, this might reflect the structural headwinds to inflation ex-energy but it also suggests more nuance in this shock than in previous episodes. records.text: 4 Europe Economic Weekly | 27 March 2026 The macroeconomic backdrop also appears more "benign" now (though we would argue it is actually more fragile to the downside) given we don’t have the pent-up demand seen back then, nor the labour shortages. Demand-supply imbalances then were a lot more pronounced, including the policy mix, and the starting point for inflation was a lot higher. We would also add that we are probably a bit less sensitive to energy price shocks overall given the efforts to diversify away from fossil energy in the past few years. On the other hand, we now have a fresher memory of inflation than back in 2022, and the response of firms and workers may be faster than last time. This is certainly true and something worth monitoring, but we would add that memory works both ways. Indeed, as we cover in the Euro-area piece, memories of the recent episode could also explain why the risk of non‑linearities in the shock transmission to the real economy is something we need to monitor closely. These risks apply to both the demand (consumers) and supply side (companies) and can play an important role not only for the near-term outlook but also for the medium-term one, even for inflation. We could easily end up with much higher savings structurally, and a persistent shock to investment, exacerbating the chronic insufficiency of aggregate demand in the region. Asia is already tighten- ing as pre-closure cargoes fade; Southeast Asia demand could drop ~300 kbd in April and potentially exceed 2 mbd in May and near 3 mbd by June if OECD stock releases stay domes- tic. Africa faces uneven risk, with up to ~250 kbd demand losses possible in April. Europe is more insulated by invento- ries and alternative supplies, so price-driven demand destruc- tion is more likely than outright shortages despite ~1.1 mbd at risk. The US will mainly feel price/refined-product disloca- tions first, though California could face supply issues by late April/May (Oil Flash Note, Mar 26th). Iran’s halt in gas exports to Türkiye after Israel’s strike on South Pars is a regional supply disruption with likely limited spillover to global LNG and only modest impact on European gas prices.Reports indicate Iran–Türkiye flows have stopped; Iran delivered ~8.2 Bcm to Türkiye in 2025 (vs. 9.4 Bcm/year in 2021–22), and January imports were only ~4 Mcm/day, well below seasonal norms. TTF front- month rose about €1.5/MWh intraday, consistent with expec- tations that Türkiye can backfill via higher Russian pipeline imports. Based on 2025 conditions, spare capacity—especial- ly on TurkStream 1—should be sufficient to offset lost Irani- an volumes, with only limited spot needs potentially appear- ing in July–August after typical June maintenance.
